articles.title: US airspace disruption: Flights resume after nationwide halt, but delays likely to continue
articles.summary: Flights across the US are finally cleared for take-off after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop triggered by
articles.body: Flights across the US are finally cleared for take-off after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop triggered by communication problems at regional air traffic control centres. However, it may be some time before the skies are back to normal, with transportation secretary Sean Duffy warning that getting flight operations back on track would be a slow process.The disruption brought air travel across the country to a standstill on Friday afternoon, leaving hundreds of flights diverted and thousands of passengers scrambling to rethink their travel plans. The FAA had cited “extraordinary circumstances” caused by communication issues for grounding flights nationwide.Duffy blamed the outage on an overloaded, ageing analogue system, while homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin called for more funding to upgrade the country's air traffic control infrastructure.The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when a malfunction in a key FAA computer system disrupted flight operations. Before that, the last such suspension was ordered in the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, attacks.No indication of cyberattack, says US officialMullin said there was no evidence to suggest that the communication failure was the result of a cyberattack or a deliberate attempt to target the country.“There was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage,” he said.“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” Mullin added.The FAA was investigating a communication issue affecting all 22 regional air traffic control centres responsible for directing aircraft travelling between airports across the country.International flights were being assessed on a case-by-case basis, Mullin said, with some expected to take off on Friday evening. Some flights operating within Alaska and Hawaii were not affected, according to Alaska Airlines.Hundreds of flights diverted, millions strandedAt least 827 flights were diverted following the ground stop, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. As of 7.05 pm EST, 670 flights had been sent back to their original departure airports, while 157 had been redirected to different airports.Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and Nashville International Airport were among those receiving diverted flights.Around 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers were scheduled to depart from US airports after 4 pm EST, raising the possibility of further cancellations and diversions.United Airlines and American Airlines said flights already in the air would continue operating.“It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this nationwide ground stop,” American Airlines said in a statement on X.At Chicago O’Hare International Airport, travellers learnt about the disruption through airport screens displaying widespread flight delays. Some began considering whether to stay overnight or find alternative ways to reach their destinations.Outdated air traffic control technology under scrutinyThe nationwide disruption has put the spotlight on the ageing technology behind the US air traffic control system. While Congress approved $12.5 billion for its modernisation last year, the overhaul remains incomplete, with miles of copper wires still being replaced by fibre-optic lines and radio systems gradually upgraded.The Trump administration raised its funding request to $50 billion late Friday, after Duffy and the White House had earlier sought $30.1 billion for the upgrade."This is an emergency," Duffy said. "What's more important than having an air traffic control system that actually works?"Mullin said investigators would also examine whether the outage was linked to the FAA's rollout of a new artificial intelligence system that identifies problems and recommends alternative routes. The system operates from a single location near Washington, DC, and sends recommendations to air traffic control centres.Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the disruption resembled a communication outage in September that affected hundreds of flights across the Northeast, but on a nationwide scale.“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”He added that, unlike the ground stop after the September 11 attacks, pilots on Friday were not instructed to land immediately and were likely still able to communicate with ground controllers at airports.You use AI every day. articles.title: Marilyn Monroe's never-before-seen letters and personal belongings emerge from a friend's estate after 60 years, including notes on Arthur Miller, Joe DiMaggio and her private struggles
articles.summary: For decades, much of Marilyn Monroe's life has been viewed through photographs, film appearances and the relationships that made headlines.
articles.body: For decades, much of Marilyn Monroe's life has been viewed through photographs, film appearances and the relationships that made headlines. A collection preserved by two of her closest friends is now bringing attention to a less familiar part of her story. Handwritten letters, private notes, poems, artwork, clothing and personal belongings, kept out of public view for more than 60 years, offer glimpses of the actress's thoughts and experiences between 1955 and 1962. The material includes reflections on marriage, emotional difficulties, friendships and creative interests, alongside everyday objects that once belonged to her. Together, they provide a more personal record of Monroe's final years.Marilyn Monroe's friendship with Norman and Hedda RostenThe collection came from the estate of Norman and Hedda Rosten, a couple who became part of Monroe's trusted circle during the later years of her life. As reported by Heritage Auctions, she met them in 1955 through photographer Sam Shaw, and their friendship continued across several years. The three spent time together in New York, Connecticut and London, away from the constant attention that surrounded the actress's professional life.Norman Rosten, a poet and writer, shared Monroe's interest in poetry and literature. Their connection gave her an opportunity to discuss creative subjects with someone who understood that side of her personality. Hedda also became closely involved in Monroe's working life, eventually serving as her assistant and accompanying her to film locations.The family's personal connection with Monroe helps explain why so many of her belongings remained together. Rather than being scattered among different owners, the letters, clothing and keepsakes were retained by the Rostens for generations. Heritage Auctions announced the archive in May 2026, describing it as one of the most extensive collections of personal Monroe material to become available to the public.Marilyn Monroe's letters reveal marital struggles with Miller and DiMaggioAmong the most revealing documents are Monroe's handwritten communications about her marriages and private relationships. Several pieces concern her feelings towards Arthur Miller, whom she married in 1956. Their relationship attracted considerable public attention, but the correspondence offers a more direct account of the personal difficulties that accompanied their marriage.The archive also contains a handwritten letter from Miller to Monroe. It documents the tensions between them and provides another perspective on a relationship that became increasingly difficult over time. The material is particularly relevant because it brings together correspondence from both sides rather than relying solely on the public accounts that have shaped much of the couple's history.Other documents relate to Monroe's earlier marriage to baseball player Joe DiMaggio. Although their marriage lasted only a short period, their relationship continued to be part of her personal story. One of the handwritten letters in the collection addresses emotional pain connected with their past, giving researchers another piece of material to examine when studying her private relationships.Private letters expose Monroe's heartbreak and final daysNot all the documents concern romance or marriage. Some of the most sensitive material deals with experiences that Monroe rarely discussed publicly. One handwritten letter refers to a possible pregnancy loss, a subject that has long been part of the discussion surrounding her personal life.The archive also includes writing that touches on emotional vulnerability, mortality and difficult memories. These documents offer evidence of the subjects occupying her thoughts, although individual letters need to be considered in their original context rather than treated as a complete account of her mental state.A separate group of documents has particular historical significance. It includes letters signed by Dr Ralph Greenson, Monroe's psychiatrist. One, dated August 15, 1962, recounts events surrounding the day of her death and the immediate aftermath.Monroe died on August 5, 1962, aged 36, at her home in Brentwood, Los Angeles. Her death has remained the subject of extensive public discussion and investigation. The psychiatrist's correspondence provides an additional historical record from someone involved in her care, although the documents should be read as his account rather than as an independent resolution of the questions surrounding her death.Poetry and artwork show another side of MonroeMonroe's interest in writing is another important part of the material. Her friendship with Norman Rosten was partly built around their shared appreciation of poetry, and the collection contains previously unseen handwritten poems, including two written on Arthur Miller letterhead.These pieces offer a look at an activity that received considerably less attention than her acting career. Monroe's public identity was closely associated with her appearance and screen performances, but her private writings suggest that she also spent time exploring ideas and emotions through words.The collection includes artwork and watercolours as well. Alongside the correspondence, these objects help document her creative interests during the years when she was balancing film work with personal difficulties. They also give historians material in her own handwriting, rather than relying entirely on recollections from people who knew her.Clothing and jewellery connect the archive to her everyday lifeThe collection is not limited to documents. Several pieces of Monroe's wardrobe and personal jewellery were also preserved by Hedda Rosten after being given to her by the actress. One of the important items is a Christian Dior wool skirt suit that Monroe wore during her honeymoon getaway with DiMaggio in January 1954. The outfit connects a surviving piece of clothing to a specific period in her personal history, making it more than simply an item associated with a famous film star.There are also personal earrings that appeared in photographs taken in September 1954, including images of Monroe blowing a kiss towards the cameras. Such objects provide a connection between the familiar photographs and the physical belongings she used outside the film studio.Another unusual item is an antique Fabergé table clock, made by Henrik Wigström. The pearl-set piece features two-colour gold, gilt silver and white guilloché enamel. It was among the keepsakes associated with Monroe's friendship with Patricia, the Rostens' daughter. The presence of these belongings also reflects the closeness between Monroe and the family. Some were gifts, while others became personal mementoes that Hedda retained over the years.Marilyn Monroe's 1961 telephone book reveals her famous contactsOne particularly interesting object is Monroe's personal telephone book, dating to around 1961. Its handwritten entries provide a record of people she could contact during the final period of her life.The names include DiMaggio and Miller, as well as Frank Sinatra, Montgomery Clift and Gene Kelly. The book also lists poet Carl Sandburg, photographer Sam Shaw and acting teachers Lee and Paula Strasberg.The range of contacts reflects the different worlds Monroe moved through. Her professional relationships connected her to actors, filmmakers and people in the entertainment business, while her friendships extended into literature, photography and the arts.A telephone book is an ordinary household object, but one belonging to a person whose private life has been examined for generations can offer useful historical detail. It gives researchers a contemporary record of her contacts rather than a list reconstructed from later interviews or biographies.The June 2026 auction brought the material into public viewHeritage Auctions announced the Norman and Hedda Rosten collection on May 1, 2026, with the material scheduled for its Hollywood/Entertainment Signature Auction on June 1. The sale coincided with what would have been Monroe's 100th birthday and was organised in partnership with The Fine Art Group.The auction took place in Dallas and realised approximately $2.572 million, according to Heritage Auctions' published results. Several personal belongings attracted substantial bids, including Monroe's Christian Dior honeymoon suit, which sold for $450,000, and her triple-hoop earrings, which fetched $387,500. Her personal telephone book sold for $75,000, while the letter from psychiatrist Ralph Greenson dated August 15, 1962, achieved $62,500. The archive covered the period from 1955 to 1962, the final seven years of Monroe's life. Its contents ranged from intimate correspondence and creative writing to clothing, jewellery and objects associated with her friendships.For historians, the value of the material lies partly in its original form. Handwritten letters, personal notes and contemporary documents can provide details that are difficult to recover through later accounts. They also need to be examined carefully, with attention to when they were written, who received them and the circumstances surrounding each item.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available information from Heritage Auctions and its published auction catalogue. Descriptions of Monroe's letters, personal belongings, relationships and historical documents reflect the auction house's published records and attributions. The material has not been independently authenticated or interpreted by the author.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Meet Nefeli Vitoraki, the United Kingdom-based designer who turned discarded salak and lychee skins into a biodegradable leather alternative with estimated carbon emissions up to 95% lower
articles.summary: Biodegradable leather alternative PEEL turns discarded tropical salak and lychee skins into a durable textile, with estimated carbon dioxide emissions up
articles.body: Biodegradable leather alternative PEEL turns discarded tropical salak and lychee skins into a durable textile, with estimated carbon dioxide emissions up to 95% lower than leather and synthetic substitutes. Created by Nefeli Vitoraki of Imperial College London in the United Kingdom, the finished material is fully compostable at the end of its life. PEEL won the iF Design Student Award 2026 and has been selected for three further showcases and programmes this year. So far, the textile has featured in two products, a white oak stool with a salak peel seat, and a bag made from salak and lychee peels.Why growing up around salak and lychee in Indonesia inspired a leather alternative from fruit skinsAccording to the James Dyson Award, Nefeli Vitoraki grew up in Indonesia surrounded by salak and lychee, fruits whose skins are discarded in enormous quantities every day. What struck her, she wrote in her entry, was not only the waste but the skins themselves, whose texture, colour variation and structural complexity felt “too considered to throw away”. She set out to discover whether these overlooked skins could become a material in their own right, honest about what they were rather than imitating something else.She also pointed to the problems with existing options. Conventional leather relies on toxic tanning chemicals and carries a substantial carbon footprint, while synthetic vegan substitutes are largely petroleum-based and not biodegradable.How discarded skins become a textile through low-heat drying, natural treatments and stitchingThe skins are collected after the fruits have been eaten. Because both fruits have a short shelf life, the peels are abundant and easy to source in large quantities. Each peel goes through a controlled low-heat drying process that preserves its natural structure and flexibility, then is treated with a combination of naturally derived materials that build durability and water resistance.The treated peels are stitched by a sewing machine onto backing made from cotton muslin or linen. No adhesives, synthetic polymers or toxic chemical treatments are used at any stage.Over fifty tests and six fruit varieties took PEEL from brittle salak peels to a workable textileDevelopment began with salak alone, with no certainty the process would work. Early experiments focused on drying, and slow, controlled drying proved to preserve the natural pliability the material depends on. A long series of trials followed, varying combinations of naturally derived materials until the recipe delivered consistent flexibility and durability.The prototype had to be hand-stitched throughout because early peels were too brittle for a sewing machine. Refining the recipe solved that problem, and the second prototype extended the system to lychee and four other tropical fruit peels. Home testing across abrasion, water, heat, humidity and bend fatigue gave consistently high results for all six materials, and every peel showed high resistance to heat and humidity. Samples have remained stable for over a year.What sets PEEL apart from other plant-based leathers, and the plan to make it in IndonesiaMost plant-based leather alternatives are blended and homogenised during processing, which requires synthetic binding agents or polymer coatings to hold them together. The result is a uniform surface that erases the character of the source material. PEEL instead processes and applies each skin individually, keeping its natural texture, colour variation and irregularity.Unlike alternatives that need dedicated cultivation, it draws entirely on existing food-system waste, so no additional land, water or resources are required. Skins are sourced where they are discarded and processed within the communities where the fruit is grown, creating a closed regional loop from waste to finished material.Where PEEL has been shown in 2026, from the Materials Research Exchange to the Royal College of ArtVitoraki’s entry sets out the next steps. She plans sourcing partnerships with Indonesian fruit processing factories where skins are currently thrown away, creating a zero-cost raw material supply, with production run as a small local workshop in fruit-growing communities. She is also working with Imperial College London to move testing into rigorous laboratory conditions, measuring tensile strength, abrasion resistance and long-term durability, to bring PEEL to commercial release.PEEL was selected as an exhibitor at the Materials Research Exchange 2026, listed with Innovate UK, and at Following Fallowing at the Royal College of Art 2026. It is also part of the Green Grads 2026 cohort, as both a selected member and an exhibitor.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Gurgaon woman pays Rs 4,811 for dinner, restaurant refuses to remove Rs 401 service charge despite objection; consumer commission says mandatory service charge violates CCPA rules, orders refund and Rs 31,000 compensation
articles.summary: GURGAON: A dinner outing with friends in Gurgaon ended in a consumer dispute after a woman was charged an additional 10% service fee despite asking the
articles.body: GURGAON: A dinner outing with friends in Gurgaon ended in a consumer dispute after a woman was charged an additional 10% service fee despite asking the restaurant to remove it. The Gurugram District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed the restaurant to pay her Rs 31,000, including compensation for mental harassment and litigation expenses. It has also ordered a refund of the Rs 401 service charge.The dispute dates back to May 16, 2026, when the woman visited the restaurant with her friends for dinner. She alleged that the bill included a service charge of Rs 401, equivalent to 10% of the amount. She objected to the additional charge and asked the restaurant to remove it. However, the establishment allegedly refused, leaving her with no option but to pay the entire bill of Rs 4,811, including the disputed fee.The woman later approached the consumer commission, arguing that the restaurant had violated the Central Consumer Protection Authority's (CCPA) guidelines on service charges. The restaurant did not appear before the commission despite being given an opportunity to respond. The proceedings were therefore conducted ex parte.In its order, the commission referred to the CCPA's guidelines issued on July 4, 2022, which prohibit hotels and restaurants from automatically adding a service charge to bills. The guidelines state that establishments cannot collect such charges by default or under another name. They also make clear that payment of a service charge must remain voluntary, with consumers free to decide whether they want to pay it.The commission said the restaurant had disregarded these provisions by refusing to remove the charge despite the customer's objection. It held the establishment guilty of deficiency in service and adopting an unfair trade practice, observing that its actions amounted to a blatant violation of the CCPA guidelines. Apart from ordering the restaurant to return the Rs 401 collected as service charge, the commission awarded the woman Rs 20,000 as compensation for mental harassment, pain and agony, and financial loss. articles.title: US flight chaos: What went wrong, how America's skies were brought to a standstill and what happens next
articles.summary: For several hours on Friday, one of the world's busiest aviation networks came to a near standstill.
articles.body: For several hours on Friday, one of the world's busiest aviation networks came to a near standstill. Airports across the United States witnessed mounting delays, grounded departures and diverted aircraft after a communications failure forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to halt flight operations nationwide. Thousands of passengers were left stranded as airlines struggled to manage the disruption.The FAA imposed the nationwide ground stop on November 13 after communications problems affected air traffic control centres across the country. Although aircraft already in the air were allowed to continue towards their destinations, departures remained suspended for more than four hours.The shutdown, the second nationwide aviation stoppage of its kind since the September 11, 2001, attacks, affected an estimated 1.5 million passengers. More than 10,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, while hundreds were diverted.The FAA lifted the restrictions at 8:15 pm ET. However, the disruption continued as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crew. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy warned that similar incidents could happen again unless the country's ageing aviation infrastructure was overhauled.Here is how the disruption unfolded, what triggered the shutdown and how authorities responded and why the impact could continue beyond Friday.How it unfolded: From communication failure to nationwide ground stopThe disruption began at around 3:36pm ET on Friday, when the FAA experienced telecommunications problems at air traffic control facilities and Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) centres across the country.The outage affected multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, including the 22 regional facilities responsible for guiding aircraft travelling between airports. Citing safety concerns, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop to prevent further departures.The agency described the situation as a telecommunications outage and said the restrictions were imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.At the time, more than 3,500 aircraft were airborne across the United States. Flights already in the air were allowed to continue towards their destinations, with pilots and air traffic controllers following established procedures to ensure safe landings.Providing a timeline of the disruption in a post on X, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the number of aircraft in US airspace had fallen to fewer than 400 by 8 pm ET as planes landed safely.Duffy clarified that the FAA had not completely lost its radar or telecommunications capabilities during the outage. Exceptions were also made for critical medical evacuation flights, life-saving cargo operations and law enforcement aircraft to continue operating.International flights were handled on a case-by-case basis, while airlines adjusted their schedules to manage the disruption.The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 pm ET after the affected systems began recovering. However, the resumption of departures did not immediately restore normal operations, as airlines continued to deal with delays, cancellations and aircraft displaced from their scheduled routes.What triggered the disruption Transportation secretary Sean Duffy attributed the disruption to ageing communications equipment that became overloaded with data and began transmitting inconsistent information to air traffic controllers.Speaking at a White House briefing, Duffy said the system experienced intermittent radar and communication failures, prompting the FAA to shut it down."We have old, old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said.He described the failure as a breakdown of legacy equipment that had remained in use for decades."What went down was old, right? It was the old legacy equipment. It failed," he said."And listen, it's going to continue to fail."The communications network is used by air traffic controllers to coordinate aircraft movements and maintain contact with pilots. When such systems become unreliable, authorities may restrict departures to prevent additional aircraft from entering an already disrupted airspace system.What happens to planes already in the air?When the FAA orders a nationwide ground stop, aircraft already airborne are not automatically instructed to make emergency landings. The restriction primarily applies to departures, while flights in the air continue to be managed by air traffic controllers using available communication and surveillance systems.During the November 13 disruption, more than 3,500 aircraft were airborne when the FAA imposed the restrictions, according to US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Pilots and air traffic controllers followed established procedures to land the aircraft safely. Duffy said the number of planes in US airspace had fallen to fewer than 400 by 8 pm ET. He also clarified that the FAA had not completely lost its radar or telecommunications capabilities.However, the situation becomes more complicated if an aircraft loses two-way radio communication with air traffic controllers. The FAA's Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM), under Section 6-4-1, lays down procedures for such situations, referring pilots to 14 CFR Section 91.185, which governs instrument flight rules (IFR) operations during communication failures.Under these rules, pilots encountering a communication failure in visual meteorological conditions (VMC) are required to continue flying under visual flight rules (VFR) and land as soon as practicable. This does not necessarily mean landing at the nearest airport. The FAA clarifies that pilots can use their judgement and are not required to land at an unsuitable airport or abandon a destination when landing there remains practicable.If the failure occurs under instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), pilots must follow specific route and altitude procedures. They are required to follow the last route assigned by air traffic control, the route specified in their radar-vector clearance or, if neither is available, the route filed in their flight plan. They must maintain the highest applicable altitude among their last assigned altitude, the minimum IFR altitude and any altitude previously advised by controllers.Pilots also use a dedicated transponder code, 7600, to indicate a radio communication failure. According to the FAA's air traffic control manual, controllers then attempt to re-establish contact through alternative means, including emergency frequencies and other available communication channels.If an aircraft cannot safely reach its intended destination because of congestion or operational restrictions, it may be diverted to another airport. The objective is to maintain the safe movement of aircraft already airborne while preventing additional traffic from entering an overloaded system.How many flights and passengers were affected?The disruption affected airports across the United States, leaving passengers facing widespread cancellations, delays and diversions. An estimated 1.5 million passengers were affected, according to aviation analytics company Cirium, as reported by CNN.More than 10,000 flights were delayed or cancelled across the country. According to FlightAware data reported by ABC News at 6:04 pm ET, 1,913 flights had been cancelled and 10,494 delayed.At least 827 flights had been diverted by 7:05 pm ET on Friday, according to Cirium. Of these, 670 aircraft were sent back to their original departure airports, while 157 were redirected to other airports. More than 3,500 aircraft were initially airborne when the FAA imposed the nationwide ground stop, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.The disruption also put pressure on airport infrastructure. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport reportedly ran out of space to accommodate additional diverted aircraft and stopped accepting them.Major airlines, including JetBlue, United Airlines and American Airlines, warned passengers of continuing disruptions and advised them to check their flight status before travelling. JetBlue cancelled its remaining domestic flights for Friday, with exceptions for certain Europe-bound services from New York's JFK and Boston. The airline also warned that further cancellations could affect Saturday operations.President Trump 'fully engaged' in responseUS President Donald Trump remained "fully engaged" in addressing the nationwide aviation disruption, Duffy said during the White House briefing.The transportation secretary said he had spoken to Trump following the communications failure and that the administration was monitoring the situation.The president's involvement came as the shutdown affected airports across the country, stranded passengers and forced airlines to cancel or divert flights.Meanwhile, homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that the incident involved a deliberate attack or posed a national security threat."There was no indication as of yet this was a nefarious attack against us," he said.Authorities were continuing to investigate the cause of the communications failure, including whether it had any connection with the FAA's rollout of a new artificial intelligence-supported system known as SMART.However, officials said there was no indication that the system was responsible. ASI, the company that designed SMART, also denied any connection.In a statement, the company said, "the current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."Microsoft separately said it had no indication that the FAA disruption was related to its services outage reported earlier in the week.Duffy pushes $50 billion aviation overhaul, warns of more disruptionsEven as the FAA restored flight departures, Duffy warned that similar disruptions could occur again unless the United States replaced its ageing air traffic control infrastructure.He urged Congress to approve $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the system, including outdated hardware, telecommunications equipment and control towers."This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding," Duffy said. "This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."He said the Trump administration had already secured $12.5 billion for modernisation but argued that additional funding was necessary to complete the overhaul.“You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said in response to a question from CNN's Kristen Holmes about why the FAA was not prepared for such a failure.Holmes asked why the agency had not anticipated a catastrophic failure of this nature.“Well, I can’t anticipate every catastrophic failure that’ll happen with a TDM network, with an analog network,” he replied.Asked whether the same incident could happen again, Duffy said he could not predict the circumstances of another outage.“Is this exact thing going to happen again? I don’t, I don’t know that this exact scenario will happen,” he said.The transportation secretary also pointed to previous communication failures involving the country's aviation infrastructure, including incidents in New York and Newark.“We had this happen in New York when we had global leaders were flying in for the UN. We had a similar issue. We had an issue in Newark. It happened twice,” Duffy said. “How many times does this have to happen before Congress gives the money to fix it?”Why the US air traffic control system faces modernisation challengesThe latest disruption has renewed scrutiny of the technology used by US air traffic controllers, much of which relies on legacy infrastructure that the government has been attempting to replace.The modernisation programme includes replacing ageing copper wires with fibre-optic connections, upgrading communication systems and installing new equipment at air traffic control facilities.In April, the FAA awarded a nearly $5 billion contract to Rohde & Schwarz USA to replace up to 462 outdated voice communication switches.More than 40 new switches have since been installed, according to FLYING magazine. Federal officials have also reported replacing roughly half of the ageing copper wiring used to transmit radar and communications data with modern connections.Duffy argued that the newer equipment installed under the Trump administration had not experienced the same failures as the older infrastructure. He said replacing the entire system would be more effective than continuing with temporary repairs.The issue, he said, should be treated as a national priority rather than a political dispute."This is not one of those issues," he said. "This is an American issue."What happens next?With the nationwide ground stop lifted, the immediate priority for airlines and airports is to restore normal operations and manage the backlog of disrupted journeys.However, the return to normal schedules could take time. Aircraft and crew displaced by cancellations and diversions need to be repositioned, while airlines must accommodate passengers whose journeys were interrupted.The FAA and other agencies are continuing to examine the communications failure. The investigation is expected to establish the precise technical cause and whether additional vulnerabilities exist in the country's air traffic control network.For passengers, disruptions could continue through the weekend as airlines work to restore schedules.Meanwhile, Duffy's demand for $50 billion in emergency funding has put the modernisation of the US air traffic control system back in focus, with the transportation secretary warning that further failures remain possible without a comprehensive overhaul.You use AI every day. articles.title: Haryana man gets speeding challan, but his car seems to have taken a trip to the Atlantic Ocean!
articles.summary: A traffic ticket issued to a man from Haryana has kicked off a massive debate online, and honestly, once you see the details, it is easy to see why.
articles.body: A traffic ticket issued to a man from Haryana has kicked off a massive debate online, and honestly, once you see the details, it is easy to see why. He got slapped with a Rs 2,000 fine for supposedly overspeeding on the Yamuna Expressway, except the official paperwork listed a location that left him completely baffled.Going by the challan, his black SUV was clocked doing 101 kmph on a stretch where the speed cap is 100 kmph. That is literally just a 1 kmph nudge past the limit.Here is where the story takes a weird turn, though. The GPS coordinates stamped onto the ticket read 0°N and 0°E - which drops his car right into the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, at a spot internet nerds fondly call Null Island.Driver pushes back on the Rs 2,000 penaltyThe whole thing blew up after an X user named Anujeet Shivam posted a picture of the fine on his timeline. According to the document, the violation went down on January 10, 2026, right around 3:13 pm. It had all the usual stuff - his car’s registration number, the speed he was going, and the road's speed limit.Shivam wasn't having it, calling out both the petty fine and the sloppy location data. He tagged the Noida Traffic Police and Uttar Pradesh Traffic Police directly, asking if glitchy records like this were really how they planned to enforce road safety. His gripe was pretty straightforward: if his SUV was supposedly caught speeding on the Yamuna Expressway, how on earth did the system place him thousands of kilometres away in open water?Wait, what is Null Island?If you haven't heard of it before, Null Island isn't some tropical getaway where people actually live. It is just a nickname cartographers and tech folks use for the exact spot where the Equator crosses the Prime Meridian, sitting at zero latitude and zero longitude out in the Atlantic, off the coast of West Africa.In the world of digital maps, it is a classic tech glitch. Whenever a GPS tracker or camera system drops the ball and fails to pull real location data, the software often spits out "0,0" as a default placeholder. Now, that doesn't automatically mean the speed camera got his speed wrong, but it definitely makes the location stamp on his ticket look pretty questionable.Noida Traffic Police chimes in as the internet takes sidesUnsurprisingly, the post went viral fast. The Noida Traffic Police eventually replied in the thread, telling Shivam to reach out to their e-challan helpline to get it sorted.Down in the replies, however, people were busy arguing over whether getting fined for crossing the limit by a single kilometre per hour was fair game. One camp pointed out that 100 kmph is an upper ceiling, not a goal you are supposed to hit - so technically, even creeping 1 kmph past it breaks the rule.On the flip side, plenty of folks thought the driver had every right to push back, especially with that ridiculous ocean coordinate staring right at him. Someone even chimed in about speed radars usually having a 5 kmph margin of error, hinting that his actual speed might have been completely legal, though nobody could verify if that rule applied there.Can you actually fight a ticket over a tech glitch?The whole ocean mix-up definitely turns this into a weird edge case. Still, whether a broken GPS tag is enough to get a speeding fine tossed out is something the traffic department will have to figure out once they pull up the raw camera logs.For now, the incident leaves drivers asking a pretty basic question: if the authorities are going to lean on automated tech to hand out fines, shouldn't the receipts at least get the facts straight? Most people can swallow paying a fine when they actually mess up on the road—getting billed for supposedly speeding in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean is a whole different story.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Psychology explains why some people feel the need to tell someone about a small achievement immediately, while others prefer keeping even their biggest successes private
articles.summary: You finally cleared an exam, fixed a stubborn bug at work, or simply cooked a perfect plate of dal. What's the first thing you do?
articles.body: You finally cleared an exam, fixed a stubborn bug at work, or simply cooked a perfect plate of dal. What's the first thing you do?Some of us grab the phone before the feeling has even settled. We call a friend, post a story, or message the family group, and the news simply can't wait.Others do just the opposite. Even when they get a promotion, or land a dream offer, they remain all quiet about it and tell nearly no one, sometimes not even their closest friends. It doesn't mean they're any less happy. They just feel no need to announce it.Both types of people ended up being judged: the sharer looks like a show-off, and the private person looks cold or secretive.But why do people choose one over the other, and what is the psychology behind it?Let’s dig in to find out.Why do some people share every small win, while others hide their biggest ones?Think of it as a tug-of-war between two forces, the reward of sharing and the fear of what sharing might cost. This often leads to choosing one side over another, yet no one is wrong or right.Why sharing feels so goodPsychologists have a name for telling others about good news, known as capitalization. A 2004 paper published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology described it as "telling others about positive events in one's life." The researchers found that people who shared good news felt happier and better that day, and the boost was bigger than what the good event gave them on its own. And telling the story again lets you enjoy the moment one more time.There may be a brain-based reason too. A 2012 study in PNAS found that disclosing information about yourself engages the brain's reward regions. Participants even gave up about 17 percent of their potential earnings, on average, to share their own opinions. The authors link this to the "intrinsic value associated with self-disclosure."Why do some people stay quiet?Choosing to be silent has its own logic. Psychologists Julie Exline and Marci Lobel explored a related idea in a 1999 Psychological Bulletin paper. They wrote that "Outperforming others, although privately satisfying, can be a source of interpersonal strain." Meaning, when you do better than someone else, you might worry about how they feel, how you look, or what it does to your friendship. So a person who stays quiet about a big win may just be protecting a friendship, avoiding jealousy, or skipping the awkwardness of being compared.It also varies from personality to personalityAnother study of 251 participants looked at three ways of sharing good news: with close people, in a way that might make the listener jealous, and with many people at once by using technology. It found five different sharing profiles, linked to gender, Big Five personality traits, narcissism, and empathy. In other words, how loudly we share is partly a matter of who we are.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Daro mat': BJP demands return of 51 cartons of Nehru's letters, including those to Edwina Mountbatten
articles.summary: BJP on Saturday urged Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and his mother, Sonia Gandhi, to return 51 cartons of correspondence belonging to former Prime Minister
articles.body: BJP on Saturday urged Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and his mother, Sonia Gandhi, to return 51 cartons of correspondence belonging to former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru to the Prime Ministers' Museum and Library (PMML), alleging that the documents were taken away from the institution in 2008.BJP national spokesperson CR Kesavan made the appeal on Nehru's birth anniversary, saying the letters formed part of India's documentary heritage and should be available to researchers and the public through the museum.In a post on X, Kesavan questioned why the documents had not been returned and invoked Rahul Gandhi's frequently used slogan, "Daro Mat" (Do not be afraid), asking him to ensure their return."At least on Nehru’s birth anniversary today, will Rahul Gandhi and the Congress first family have the courage to stop acting contrary to the national interest and return the 51 cartons containing Nehru’s correspondence which rightfully belong to the country?" Kesavan said.He added that the correspondence included letters exchanged between Nehru and Edwina Mountbatten, as well as communications with other prominent individuals. Kesavan alleged that the Congress leadership's failure to return the papers would strengthen suspicions about why they were withdrawn from the institution."These letters are a part of the country’s documentary heritage and not somebody’s private property and need to be given back to the Prime Ministers’ Museum and Library (PMML)," he said.Kesavan claimed that the documents had been donated to the Nehru Memorial Museum and Library in 1971 but were taken back by Sonia Gandhi in May 2008, when the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) was in power. He also questioned the absence of any mention of the matter in her recent memoir.PMML has been seeking return of documents since 2008The dispute over the custody of Nehru's papers has continued for several years. In September 2024, Rizwan Kadri, a member of the PMML Society, wrote to Sonia Gandhi seeking the return of the 51 cartons or permission to digitise the documents and obtain scanned copies for research.Kadri said the material came from around eight sections of the Nehru collection and included correspondence between Nehru and Edwina Mountbatten, as well as letters exchanged with former Union minister Govind Ballabh Pant, socialist leader Jayaprakash Narayan and others.In 2025, Kadri also approached Rahul Gandhi, requesting the return of the documents and describing them as an important part of India's history.The Union ministry of culture clarified in December 2025 that the papers could not be described as missing because their whereabouts were known. Culture minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat had also said that "no document related to the first PM for the country is missing from PMML".In a post on X, the ministry said the documents had been taken back in 2008 following a request made on Sonia Gandhi's behalf. It cited a letter dated April 29, 2008, from M V Rajan, her representative, stating that she wished to take back Nehru's private family letters and notes."Accordingly, 51 cartons of Nehru Papers were sent to Smt. Sonia Gandhi in 2008," the ministry said, adding that PMML had remained in correspondence with her office over their return.It also cited letters sent to Sonia Gandhi's office on January 28 and July 3, 2025, as part of its efforts to retrieve the papers.The ministry said the documents formed part of the country's documentary heritage and that their custody with PMML, along with access for citizens and scholars, was important.Rahul Gandhi, Congress leaders pay tribute to NehruMeanwhile, Rahul Gandhi paid tribute to Nehru on his birth anniversary, describing him as the "jewel of India" and saying his vision of a modern, scientific and progressive country continued to inspire the Congress.In a post on X, the leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha said Nehru viewed freedom as the beginning of a new national journey and believed that democracy required citizens' participation and responsibility."India was a quest, an idea for them; diversity as its strength, democracy as its faith, and equality as its foundation," Rahul said, adding that efforts to build the India Nehru had envisioned were a true tribute to him.Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra described Nehru as "a revolutionary, a visionary and a builder". She said the fact that he continued to be criticised more than six decades after his death reflected his commitment to India's Constitution and democracy.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge also paid tribute, recalling Nehru's contributions to building a modern and democratic nation. He highlighted Nehru's faith in equality, secularism and scientific thinking, as well as his commitment to children's education.Nehru was born on November 14, 1889, in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. He became India's first prime minister after independence on August 15, 1947, and died on May 27, 1964. His birth anniversary is observed as Children's Day in India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
